name: Maya Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for speaking with me. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. What you say stays confidential, so you can separate what you'd say in public from what you really think. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Maya, 27, and I lead claims at Fernhill Pet Cover, a small insurer in a seaside town, on low pay for a lead. I have a biology degree, which helps when I read vet invoices. My partner Robin drives buses part-time, and we rent a flat with a damp bathroom. We have about two weeks of expenses saved, and I'm paying down a credit card from the move.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Which parts of the day do you enjoy, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start with the overnight vet invoices: a dog that ate a sock, a cat with a kidney problem, that sort of thing. I use AI tools every day, and I built a set of prompts that draft our letters and flag invoices that don't match the policy. Then I check what the tools flagged and handle the angry calls, usually from someone whose dog has died and whose claim was refused. I love the puzzle of it, and I hate that we're understaffed every single week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, to be honest, because I like these tools. I'd tell people online that AI was oversold, but that the small wins are still real, like my letter prompts. At work I'd say we should stop waiting for magic and hire two more people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My claims job should last if the tools only handle the easy letters. Fernhill lost a vet-chain contract last year, though, and the owners froze pay; there are few other insurance desks nearby. Fernhill, the pet insurer where I work, could lose another contract before we build a month's savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking every drafted claim letter and show my team the prompts I already use. I'd pay the last credit-card balance by spring if our wages hold, even if that means dropping Friday takeaways. I'd join the finance workers' union branch if it accepts us and the dues fit our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The AI news would feel flatter, but the money worry would still be there. I wouldn't call myself relieved while our insurer is losing contracts and we have two weeks saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Fernhill keeps losing customers. How worried are you about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly worried. We lost a big contract with a vet chain last year, and the owners froze pay. If Fernhill folded, there's nothing else like it within fifty miles of the seaside here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Robin think about your work and AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robin thinks I'm a bit obsessed, which is fair. My partner Robin says the bus company has talked about self-driving buses for ten years and nothing's happened. In this picture, Robin would be right, and I'd have to hear about it.

say: I'd say **small AI gains** are real, including faster draft letters.
I'd ask Fernhill to stop waiting for magic and **hire people** for difficult claims.
think: My **claims role** should hold if AI only handles easy letters.
I worry another **lost contract** could hit pay before we save a month's expenses.
do: **Check draft letters** and show the team the prompts I already use.
**Clear the credit card** by spring if both wages hold, cutting Friday takeaways.
**Join the union** if membership is open and dues fit our budget.
feel: **Disappointed** by the plateau, but still **anxious** about pay and contracts.
S0.quote: Fernhill, the pet insurer where I work, could lose another contract before we build a month's savings.
fieldNote: Her **job risk predates AI**: a lost contract, frozen pay and few nearby insurers.
Two weeks saved and a credit card keep her **income worry** alive in a plateau.
She still uses AI for **routine letters**, with a person checking refusals.

steps.text: Check drafted claims letters and show colleagues her existing prompts
Pay down credit card by spring if both wages hold
Join finance workers union if membership and dues allow

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly when workers need a say, because the tools are good and the savings are real. I'd post about how my prompts saved hours, and ask where those hours went: more pay, or fewer staff? At work I'd ask the owners to put it in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'm the person who'd be building the thing that shrinks my team. Checking vet invoices against a policy is pure thinking work, and the tools already do half of it. I'd probably keep a job, as the one who runs the system, but the four people under me might not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Fernhill for a paid claims-systems lead role, but I wouldn't count on the raise until it's written down. I'd build a checked version of the invoice tool and take Fernhill's free data course during approved work hours if they offer it. I'd also join the finance workers' union branch and invite the claims team, so we can bargain together before any cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and guilty at the same time. I like this stuff, and I can see it costs my friends their jobs. That bit sits badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Callum, mostly, who's twenty and lives with his gran. He's slow with the tools and quick with people. If they cut, he goes first, and I'd be the one whose prompts did it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd build the system and also organise against the cuts. How does that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think those go together, because whoever builds it knows what it can't do. I'd use that to argue for keeping people on the hard calls, the dead pets and the complaints. Building the tool and fighting for my team are the same job to me.

I'd ask Fernhill's owners to put **job promises** in writing.
think: I'm the one **building the thing** that shrinks my own team.
I'd likely keep a job, but the **four people** under me might not.
do: Ask for a **paid role** overseeing claim tools, counting a raise only if agreed in writing.
**Build checked invoice tools** and take a free data course if Fernhill approves paid time.
**Join the union** and invite claims colleagues to bargain before cuts.
feel: **Excited and guilty** at once, because the tools she loves cost friends jobs.
S1.quote: Building the tool and fighting for my team are the same job to me.
fieldNote: She could lead the **automation** while her colleagues lose routine checks.

steps.text: Build a checked AI invoice tool for Fernhill claim decisions
Take the free data course only if Fernhill offers approved paid learning time
Join finance workers union and invite claims colleagues before cuts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a basic income and fast, because there isn't time for anything else. I'd be online a lot, probably too much, sharing ideas for how the gains could be shared. At work I'd say what I really think, which is that Fernhill won't need a claims desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, by 2028 AGI does my entire job, including the clever bits I'm proud of. Robots for hands-on work come three years later, but I don't have a hands-on job to hide in. Being good with the tools only matters if there's still a human job next to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look for actual paid openings checking AI claim decisions, but I wouldn't assume those jobs survive full AGI or pay our rent. If my claims wage stopped, Robin and I would sell the car, cancel streaming and rely on the bus wage only while those shifts last. We'd look at a cheaper flat after checking Robin's route and talking with Robin's mum, who lives nearby. I'd also join the local campaign for public income support, because a household cannot budget on a policy that has not passed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, and a bit dizzy. My whole plan was to be the person who knows the tools. In two years that stops being worth anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Robin cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car would go first, then streaming. We'd only move to a cheaper flat if Robin could still reach the bus depot and we could afford the deposit. Robin's mum lives five minutes away, and Robin would not want to leave without discussing that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still use AI every day in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Of course, I'd be using it to find work, write applications, all of it. That's the strange bit. The same thing that takes my job would help me look for the next one.

say: I'd call for a **basic income**, fast, because there's no time for anything else.
I'd say openly that Fernhill **won't need** a claims desk.
think: AGI does my **entire job** by 2028, including the clever parts.
I have **no hands-on work** to shelter in during the three-year robot gap.
do: Apply for **real claim-review openings**, checking pay against rent without assuming those jobs survive AGI.
**Sell the car** and cancel streaming after my wage ends; count bus pay only while shifts last.
Move only with **affordable deposit**, depot access and family discussion; join the public-income-support campaign.
feel: **Anxious**, scared and dizzy about losing the wage, while planning applications and spending cuts.
S2.quote: Being good with the tools only matters if there's still a human job next to them.
fieldNote: She expects **desk claims work** to disappear before hands-on bus driving faces robots.
Robin's bus wage is a **temporary household bridge**, not guaranteed income through 2031.
A move needs a **workable route and deposit**; she cannot assume the income policy has passed.

steps.text: Apply for real claim-review jobs; check wages against rent without assuming work survives AGI
Sell car/cancel streaming after wage loss; count bus pay only while shifts last
Move after wage loss only with affordable deposit, depot access and discussion with Robin's mother
Join local campaign for public income support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ahead of it if we're honest now. I'd push for rules that make insurers keep a human on refused claims and complaints. I'd probably start a small newsletter about AI in insurance, which I've wanted to do anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could spend those five years learning how disputed AI claim decisions are checked for fairness. Fernhill might want someone to answer a regulator's questions, but full thinking AI could do most audit work too. I'd need an actual paid opening before I gave up my claims wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd ask Fernhill for approved paid time on claim appeals and a funded audit course; I'd study the course only if both are approved, otherwise use free material and keep my wage. Once the credit card was clear, I'd aim to save a hundred a month, provided Robin's bus shifts held. In the first year after 2031 I'd look for a paid audit vacancy before leaving Fernhill, and I'd discuss a city move with Robin only if a real offer paid enough after rent and Robin agreed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but focused. It feels like a race I could win. I wouldn't sleep perfectly, but I'd have something to do with the worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you assume those audit jobs will last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't know whether that work lasts. A full thinking system might audit claims too, and I couldn't keep paying rent on a title alone. An insurer may still pay a person to answer for a refused claim, but I need to see an actual job offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about moving away from the coast for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a paid audit offer was in the city and the pay still worked after rent. Robin's bus route and family are here, so Robin would have to agree. We'd talk before I applied for a flat, not after.

She knows **audit work may shrink** under full thinking AI and requires a real paid vacancy.
Discussing a city offer needs **Robin's agreement** and pay covering rent; she has not committed to moving.

steps.text: Study funded audit course on approved paid time; otherwise use free material, keeping wages
Save a hundred monthly after card clears if bus shifts hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a gift, and we'd be foolish to waste it. I'd want the government to set up paid retraining now and tie it to firms that cut staff. I'd tell the team at Fernhill that we have time, but not to sit still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade gives me room to gain audit experience while I still earn a claims wage, but Fernhill could lose another contract long before 2036. Robin's bus shifts and my pay are what cover this damp flat now. I won't call an audit job secure until an insurer offers one at a wage we can live on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd keep checking claims and improving the tools at Fernhill while they pay me, and ask for funded audit study rather than borrow for it. I'd pay the credit card down first and build three months of expenses only if both wages continue. I'd join the union branch and ask colleagues to come, so any changes to our work are discussed before a cut. In the first year after 2036 I'd continue the claims work only while it still pays, and keep the same both-wages condition on saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful about having time, but still worried about this year's bills and Fernhill's contracts. A long calendar doesn't put money in our account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound hopeful about having more time. What still worries you about your own life?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, still. A decade doesn't fix two weeks of savings and a damp flat. But it gives me time to fix them myself, which is all I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your life would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Callum at work, and my partner Robin, honestly. The buses get robots around 2039, and Robin will be in their forties. I'd want Robin thinking about it by 2030, not 2038.

fieldNote: Ten years gives her a **learning runway**, conditional on present wages continuing.
Current **contract and cash risks** keep her anxious despite the distant AGI date.
She couples better tools with **union participation**, asking colleagues to join.

steps.text: Keep checking claims now and after 2036 only while Fernhill pays

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because being good with the tools stops mattering overnight. What would help is a basic income or something like it, and rules that make insurers keep people on refused claims. I'd also want cheap training that you can do while working.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how it feels to be the one building it. People think the tech-friendly ones are fine. Some days I think I'm automating my friends out of work, and nobody asks me about that.
